The rest are the EU energy tax law those permissions rest on, two road-fuel tax reliefs under the same law, and an electricity market outlook. Six members are national tax permissions of one shape, granted under the EU energy tax law to Denmark, France, Italy, Spain, Sweden and Germany. The Spanish one reads: Spain is authorised to apply a reduced taxation rate to electricity directly supplied to vessels, other than private pleasure craft, berthed in ports, provided that the minimum levels of taxation referred to in Article 10(1) of Directive 2003/96/EC are respected. The general infrastructure law sits beside them (The regulation sets mandatory national targets for road vehicles, vessels and stationary aircraft), as does Norway's rule for its heritage fjords, under which passenger ships shall use shore power where it is available. The outlook holds no figure about electricity sold to ships.","meaning":"For a freight operator with no sustainability background: a ship at berth normally burns its own fuel to make the power it needs there. Plugging into the port grid instead is called shore power. The rule-makers say why they want it: The use of shore-side electricity avoids emissions from burning bunker fuels at berth and contributes to an improvement in the local air quality in port cities and to noise reduction. Several governments have asked the EU for permission to tax electricity sold to ships at a lower rate than the law otherwise requires, and the decisions state the purpose plainly: The authorisation is granted for a four-year period so as not to discourage relevant economic operators from making the necessary investments. Italy's decision says the same in other words: In order to enable port and ship operators, as well as distributors and redistributors of electricity, to continue promoting the use of shore-side electricity, it is appropriate to authorise Italy to apply a reduced rate of taxation to shore-side electricity.

*Analytical inference:* the chain the decisions describe runs from a lower tax on quay-side electricity, to a cheaper connection for ship and port operators, to the investment the four-year term is meant to protect; a target or an obligation (inland ports must have connections, Norwegian passenger ships must plug in where a connection exists) then turns the option into a requirement. Because each permission is national and dated, the cost of quay-side power for a ship can differ by country and can change when a permission ends; the members do not state the tax rate any country actually applies.","ramifications":"### Regulations
The tax permissions are temporary and individual. They also fall away if a common EU rule arrives: should the Council, acting on the basis of Article 113 TFEU, provide for general rules on tax advantages for shore-side electricity, this Decision shall expire on the day on which those general rules become applicable. A non-binding Commission recommendation asked for the connections long before the targets: Member States should consider the installation of shore-side electricity for use by ships at berth in ports; particularly in ports where air quality limit values are exceeded. Norway goes further with money as well as rules: The Norwegian Government has allocated NOK 100 million to Aurland Port Authority for shore power infrastructure in Flåm, administered by Enova.

Two members are tax relief on road fuel rather than on electricity, granted under the same tax law: Sweden is authorised to apply a reduction of the rates up to 2,4 SEK per litre below the minimum levels of taxation referred to in Article 7 of Directive 2003/96/EC for gas oil and unleaded petrol used as motor fuels, because the application of a reduced rate of excise duty aims to alleviate the social and economic impacts of high retail prices of petrol and diesel resulting from the geopolitical situation and directly affecting both households and companies. An older permission covered taxis only: the Netherlands is authorised to apply a degressive differentiated rate of excise duty, not exceeding NLG 0,14 per litre, on diesel fuel consumed by taxis in the period 1 January to 31 December 2000.

*Operational implication:* a forwarder who books port calls or barge moves in these countries can ask carriers whether shore power is used at berth and whether the reduced tax is passed on; the members state the permission, not the carrier's practice.

### Research
The research member is an electricity market outlook, not a study of ships. Its one price outlook is for households in the United States: residential electricity prices are expected to increase by 5% in 2026. That is not the price a European port charges a ship, and no member gives that price. The same member records the grid side: ENTSO-E states that developments at the local level can have system-wide implications, and in one blackout The ENTSO-E press release says the blackout factors led to fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections.

*Analytical inference:* the rules move ships' power at berth from their own engines onto port grids country by country through the end of this decade, so the reliability of those grids becomes part of a ship's port stay; the members state the grid events, not any port's backup arrangement.","watch":"- Sweden's road-fuel tax cut ends first: This Decision shall apply from 1 July 2026 until 30 November 2026. Whether it is extended will appear on Regulations as a new Council decision.
- France's shore-power permission is the next to run out: shall apply from 1 January 2021 until 31 December 2026. A renewal would appear on Regulations as a new Council implementing decision addressed to France.
- The infrastructure law's first review is due: By 31 December 2026 and every five years thereafter, the Commission shall review this Regulation. The review also looks at whether more vessels are covered, because the review assesses a possible extension of the scope of the Regulation to other ship types. The review report would appear on Regulations.

- Inland ports face a supply deadline: at least one installation providing shore-side electricity supply to inland waterway vessels is deployed at all TEN-T comprehensive inland waterway ports by 31 December 2029.
- Norway widens its fjord rule to large passenger ships: From 1 January 2032 , the same requirement will extend to ships of 10,000 GT and above.

For airlines the free permits are gone: From 2026 onward: Full auctioning. No free allowances. Airlines must purchase all allowances at auction or on secondary markets. The market members price the inputs (the carbon permit, crude oil and jet fuel, and the alternative jet fuel), the operations members describe what the UK, Singapore, Japan and the EU core markets do at their hubs, and the research members say how far new fuels and new aircraft can go and how fast.","meaning":"For a freight operator with no sustainability background: the EU issues a limited number of permits to emit carbon dioxide, and carriers must hand in permits for what they emit. Shipping companies must purchase and surrender EU ETS emission allowances for each tonne of reported CO₂ (or CO₂ equivalent) emissions in scope. The forwarder is not the payer; there is no requirement for freight forwarders to register with an administering authority, hold a Union Registry account, or submit MRV reports. The cost reaches the forwarder through the carrier's price. For air the source says so directly: The phase-out (25% reduction in 2024, 50% in 2025, full auctioning from 2026) increases the carbon cost airlines must recover through pricing on intra-EEA routes. For ocean one capture recorded that Carriers are currently billing ETS surcharges against the September 2026 surrender obligation (70% of verified 2025 emissions). The share of a voyage that is charged depends on the route: The regulation covers 100% of emissions from voyages between two EU/EEA ports and from ships while at EU/EEA ports, while The regulation covers 50% of emissions from voyages beginning or ending outside the EU/EEA.

Cleaner fuel costs more than the fuel it replaces: ICCT puts SAF cost at 2 to 5 times fossil jet fuel. The rules pay part of that gap: 20 million ETS allowances (EUR 1.6 bn at an allowance price of EUR 80) have been reserved to cover some, or all, of the price gap between conventional fossil fuels and eligible alternative aviation fuels uplifted from January 2024.

*Analytical inference:* the permit price, times the tonnes a carrier emits on the covered part of the trip, is a carrier cost that the sources say carriers recover in fares and surcharges; cleaner fuel raises the fuel bill, which the reserved permits partly offset for airlines. A lane's carbon charge therefore moves with the permit price, with how much of the route is covered and with how much of the emissions must be covered that year; none of the members states a carrier's surcharge formula, so a charge cannot be checked against these rows alone.","ramifications":"### Regulations
The duty sits with the carrier: EU ETS aviation obligations fall on aircraft operators. For air the scope is still Europe-only: The EU decided to temporarily limit the scope of the EU ETS to flights within the EEA. For shipping the gases covered widened this year: CH₄ and N₂O enter ETS scope (surrender obligations attach) from 1 January 2026. The ship rule does not depend on the flag a ship flies: It applies to all large ships (≥5,000 gross tonnage) calling at EU/EEA ports, regardless of flag state. The last partial surrender has already passed: ETS allowance surrender for 70% of 2025 reported emissions is due by 30 September 2026.

### Market Intel
The permit price is the multiplier. Today: Live EU compliance market price is 78.23 euros, with changes of +1.93% for a period the page does not state and -15.35% year to date. Last year: 2025 average auction price EUR 73.43 and average secondary market price EUR 74.35. Fuel is a separate driver this year: Brent reached 138 dollars per barrel on April 7 and averaged 117 dollars in April after the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and the same outlook says EIA expects prices to fall as Middle East production rises, to 89 dollars a barrel in the fourth quarter and 79 dollars in 2027. Air freight prices rose at the same time (global air cargo spot rates rose 41% year-on-year in May to an average of $3.40 per kg); no member attributes any of that rise to the carbon price.

*Analytical inference:* the permit price and the fuel price are separate inputs to a carrier's cost, so a rate can rise from either; no member states how a carrier splits the two in a surcharge.

### Operations
Hubs outside the EU use their own levers. The UK sets targets (The UK's 2025 Maritime Decarbonisation Strategy targets 30% GHG reduction by 2030, 80% by 2040, and zero by 2050) but reports that No frameworks or monitoring tools are yet in place to assess progress towards net zero targets for shipping. Singapore cuts port dues for ships that switch: MPA has committed S$50 million to a refreshed MSGI running from January 2025 to December 2027, with port dues concessions of up to 100% for vessels using qualifying alternative fuels.

### Research
The research members describe how far fuels and aircraft can go. For ships: The committed emissions of the existing shipping fleet at expected turn-over with no policy interventions will exceed credible remaining carbon budgets for the sector, though Operational changes through slow-steaming, energy efficiency, shore-power and wind-propulsion with route optimisation can enable shipping to keep within Paris Agreement aligned carbon budgets. For aircraft: Near zero-carbon aircraft that can undertake transatlantic flights will unlikely be widely available until the 2040s. For the fuel: The SAF commercialisation timeline will depend on reducing the cost of production, increasing efficiencies, as well as connecting components into a system that can operate effectively to deliver SAFs at scale.

*Analytical inference:* with new aircraft for long routes not expected before the 2040s, the price gap between cleaner and fossil jet fuel is where the near-term cost of the change sits for air freight.","watch":"- The EU's check on the global airline offsetting scheme was due before this brief (By July 2026, the Commission will carry out an assessment of CORSIA to determine if it is sufficiently delivering on the goals of the Paris Agreement); no member records its result.
